mappings.note: the HEIGHT is given (75 m) and the horizontal DISTANCE is required, so the student must pick tan and then invert it. Not C-6.3-LO-3, which is the opposite direction (height from a known distance)

both sides are known (height = shadow) and the ANGLE is the unknown; the demand is recognising that the pair perpendicular/base selects tan. No height or distance is computed, so C-6.3-LO-3 does not apply
the canonical form of this outcome: a known ground distance (15 m shadow) and a measured elevation (45) give the height. Everything in the chapter's core family reduces to this

nothing is calculated: the marked 60 at the object has to be transferred to the observer's horizontal as an alternate angle and NAMED the angle of depression. Pure definition-in-a-figure

broken-tree problem: the whole difficulty is drawing it - realising the fallen piece equals the broken part so the answer is CB + DC, not one side. Once the labelled figure exists, tan 30 and cos 30 finish it. Diagram outcome first, height computation second
the 20 m rope is the HYPOTENUSE, not a ground distance, so sin must be chosen rather than the reflex tan. That choice is the whole item, which is why it is C-6.1-LO-3 and not C-6.3-LO-3
tan theta = 15/8 is not a standard angle, so sin theta = 15/17 must be built first and then matched to the 85 m hypotenuse; ratio selection plus conversion, with no elevation value ever named

two poles: the horizontal through the shorter top must be drawn so the working triangle has vertical side 20 - 14 = 6. That construction is the graded step; sin 30 then gives the wire (a hypotenuse), hence C-6.1-LO-3 rather than C-6.3-LO-3
the observer's 1.5 m eye height must be subtracted from the 22 m tower before any ratio is written - a diagram step that is the entire trap - and the unknown is then the ANGLE from tan = 20.5/20.5

POOR FIT, recorded as such: this is solved by similar triangles (6/4 = PQ/50) and no trigonometric ratio or angle appears anywhere. C-6.1-LO-3 is cited because the invariant being used IS height/shadow = tan of the sun's elevation, but no legal code in this chapter covers a similar-triangles item

one observer on a 7 m roof sights the tower's top (elevation 60) AND its foot (depression 45) - two triangles sharing the horizontal BE, which must be drawn. Nearest legal code is LO-4; strictly its text says two observers or two positions, and this is two lines of sight from one position (see defect note)

genuinely TWO observation points P and Q at distances a and b - the literal reading of LO-4 - and the complementary elevations multiply to give h = root(ab). The complementary-angle relation itself lives in chapter 8 and has no legal code here

one ground point, two elevations (45 to the building top, 60 to the tower top), so two nested triangles on a shared base; the tower height is the DIFFERENCE of two computed heights. Mapped to LO-4 as the two-angle code

assertion-reason where the Reason is verbatim the ratio-selection statement (tan = perpendicular/base) and the Assertion is the height computed from a 30 elevation and the known base 20 m. The two codes map the two halves of the item
